summary: The note describes how the town of Ashtonville mobilized from September 2023 onward to reduce pollution and improve residents' health. Triggered by children's respiratory problems and poor air quality, the community launched 'Ashtonville Breathe Easy' (ABE), with tree planting, air purifiers, bike sharing, industry changes, organic dining, school recycling and an arts festival. It stresses that environmental health is a shared responsibility and that the work is ongoing.
one_line: Ashtonville residents unite through the 'Ashtonville Breathe Easy' initiative to cut pollution and improve community health via air, transport, industry, food, school and arts efforts.
key_facts: The residents of Ashtonville have come together on environmental health since September 4, 2023.
Air quality in Ashtonville dipped to dangerous levels due to industrial emissions, as confirmed by reports on October 12, 2023.
Retired schoolteacher Martha Simmons, whose grandson Tommy was coughing profusely, became the spark for the community-wide effort.
Dr. Jameson Keller, a local environmental health advocate, led town hall meetings starting November 2, 2023.
'Ashtonville Breathe Easy' (ABE) launched on December 15, 2023, with air purifying units and a tree planting campaign.
Environmental engineer Dr. Rebecca Cho helped select pollutant-absorbing species such as Amur maple and Siberian elm.
A bicycle-sharing program was inaugurated on January 20, 2024, with local businesses offering discounts and incentives; Joe Harris traded his car keys for a bicycle pass.

Michael Thompson, owner of Ashton Industries, decided on February 8, 2024, to switch to environmentally friendly production after worker sick days from pollution-related illnesses hit an all-time high.
Restauranteur Anita Gonzalez introduced a fully organic menu on March 3, 2024, partnering with Cloverfield Organic Farms for pesticide-free produce.
A fifth-grade class at Maplewood Elementary School launched a recycling program on April 17, 2024, which later became district-wide.
The Ashtonville Arts Fest reopened on May 6, 2024, after a two-year pandemic pause, with the theme 'Art in the Time of Climate Action'.
Artist Emma Johnson created sculptures depicting the effects of pollution at the Arts Fest.
